title: Lean Enterprise Institute, Muda, Mura, Muri (Lean Lexicon)
text:
## Muda, Mura, Muri: the Three Ms of waste

The Toyota Production System attacks three distinct categories of loss, often called the Three Ms. A top operations leader knows that muda gets all the attention but mura and muri are the upstream causes: chase muda alone and it comes back.

## Muda (waste)

Muda is any activity that consumes resources without creating value for the customer. Lean distinguishes two types. Type One Muda is activity that creates no value but cannot be eliminated immediately given current technologies or assets: an example is a rework or inspection operation you cannot yet remove. Type Two Muda is activity that creates no value and can be eliminated quickly through kaizen, for example unnecessary movement of product between process steps. The practical rule: remove Type Two muda now, work steadily to design out Type One muda.

## Mura (unevenness)

Mura is unevenness in an operation: gyrating production schedules not driven by actual end-customer demand, and uneven work pacing that forces operators to alternate between rushing and waiting. Mura is reduced through level scheduling (heijunka) and by holding a consistent, steady work pace.

## Muri (overburden)

Muri is overburdening equipment or operators by requiring them to run at a harder, faster pace with more force and effort, for a longer period, than the equipment design and appropriate workforce management allow. Muri drives breakdowns, defects, injuries, and burnout.

## How the three interrelate

The three Ms are linked: eliminating one often eliminates the others. In the classic transport example, overloading one truck to save trips (muri) creates uneven flow at the receiving dock (mura) and generates the waste of waiting and rework (muda). The stable countermeasure is heijunka (level scheduling), which smooths demand so neither people nor machines are alternately starved and overloaded. Attribution: Lean Enterprise Institute Lean Lexicon.

title: Lean Enterprise Institute, Jidoka (Lean Lexicon)
text:
## Jidoka: automation with a human touch

Jidoka means providing machines and operators the ability to detect when an abnormal condition has occurred and to immediately stop work. It lets an operation build quality into each process (quality at the source) and separate human work from machine work so one operator can run several machines. Jidoka is one of the two pillars of the Toyota Production System; the other is just-in-time.

## Origin: Sakichi Toyoda and the automatic loom

Sakichi Toyoda, founder of the Toyota Group, created the concept in the early 1900s. Previously, if a thread broke, a loom would keep running and churn out mounds of defective fabric, so each machine needed its own watching operator. Toyoda invented a loom that stopped automatically the moment a thread broke, so one operator could oversee many machines at once. Preventing the defect at the instant it occurs, rather than discovering it later, is the heart of jidoka.

## Autonomation

Jidoka is sometimes called autonomation, meaning automation with human intelligence. The equipment is given enough judgment to distinguish good parts from bad autonomously, without being monitored, freeing people for higher-value multiprocess work.

## Stop, and surface the problem

Jidoka highlights the causes of problems because work stops immediately when a problem first occurs. Stopping the line (often signaled by an andon) makes the abnormality visible at once and forces root-cause problem solving instead of letting defects pass downstream. The principle: never let a defect move to the next step. Build quality in rather than inspecting it in afterward. Attribution: Lean Enterprise Institute Lean Lexicon.

title: Lean Enterprise Institute, Just-in-Time Production (Lean Lexicon)
text:
## Just-in-Time (JIT) production

Just-in-time is a system of production that makes and delivers just what is needed, just when it is needed, and just in the amount needed. Its goal is the total elimination of waste to achieve the best possible quality, the lowest possible cost and use of resources, and the shortest possible production and delivery lead times. JIT and jidoka are the two pillars of the Toyota Production System.

## The three operating elements

JIT is built on three elements working together:
1. Takt time: the rate at which product must be made in a process to meet customer demand.
2. Continuous flow: producing and moving one item at a time (or a small, consistent batch) through a series of steps as continuously as possible, with each step making only what the next step requires.
3. Pull system: a method of production control in which downstream activities signal their needs to upstream activities, so nothing is produced until the customer (internal or external) actually requests it. Kanban signals are the common tool for this.

## Heijunka as the foundation

JIT relies on heijunka (production leveling) as its foundation. Without leveling demand, a pure pull system would transmit every spike and dip straight upstream, recreating mura and muri.

## History

The concept originated with Kiichiro Toyoda in the 1930s, with practical implementation beginning around 1949 to 1950 under Taiichi Ohno. Attribution: Lean Enterprise Institute Lean Lexicon.

title: Lean Enterprise Institute, Standardized Work (Lean Lexicon)
text:
## Standardized work

Standardized work means establishing precise procedures for each operator's work in a production process, based on three elements:
1. Takt time: the rate at which products must be made in a process to meet customer demand.
2. The precise work sequence in which an operator performs tasks within takt time.
3. The standard inventory (standard in-process stock), including units held in machines, required to keep the process operating smoothly.

## Standardized work is the baseline for kaizen

Once established and displayed at the workstation, standardized work becomes the object of continuous improvement through kaizen. This is the crucial and most misunderstood point: a standard is not a straitjacket, it is the current best-known method and the baseline against which every improvement is measured. Taiichi Ohno's maxim captures it: where there is no standard, there can be no kaizen. If the method drifts or varies operator to operator, you cannot tell whether a change actually improved anything, because there is no stable reference. So standardize first, then improve the standard, then re-standardize. Standardized work also exposes abnormalities immediately: when the actual work departs from the documented sequence or in-process stock, the deviation is visible at a glance. Attribution: Lean Enterprise Institute Lean Lexicon.

title: Lean Enterprise Institute, Heijunka / Production Leveling (Lean Lexicon)
text:
## Heijunka: leveling production

Heijunka is leveling the type and quantity of production over a fixed period of time. It lets a plant meet customer demand efficiently while minimizing inventory, capital cost, labor, and production lead time across the value stream. Heijunka is the foundation that makes a just-in-time pull system stable.

## Leveling by volume

Production quantity is smoothed across the period. If a producer receives 500 orders a week arriving unevenly (200 Monday, 100 Tuesday, 50 Wednesday, 100 Thursday, 50 Friday), it can instead build a level 100 units per day, holding a small buffer of finished goods near shipping to absorb the daily swings. This protects the upstream processes from the customer's day-to-day volatility.

## Leveling by product type or mix

Rather than mass-producing one model in a big batch, the producer sequences different models through the period. A shirt maker with weekly demand of 5 of Model A, 3 of Model B, and 2 each of Models C and D would replace the batch sequence A A A A A B B B C C D D with a repeating mixed pattern such as A A B C D A A B C D A B, adjusted as orders change. Mixed sequencing shortens the replenishment interval for every model.

## The heijunka box

A heijunka box is a visual scheduling tool: product types on one axis, time intervals on the other, with kanban cards slotted to pace the leveled sequence so operators can execute it at a glance.

## Why it matters

Heijunka directly counters mura (unevenness) and muri (overburden). Batch-and-queue by contrast expands lead time, inflates work-in-process, propagates a defect across a whole batch before it is caught, and strains workers with alternating idle and rush periods. Attribution: Lean Enterprise Institute Lean Lexicon.

title: Lean Enterprise Institute, 5S (Lean Lexicon)
text:
## 5S: workplace organization and visual control

5S refers to five related terms, each beginning with an S sound, describing workplace practices conducive to visual control and lean production. The point is not tidiness for its own sake: a workplace organized so that the normal condition is obvious makes any abnormality visible instantly, which is the precondition for standard work and continuous improvement.

## The five terms

1. Seiri (Sort): separate needed from unneeded items, tools, parts, materials, paperwork, and discard the unneeded.
2. Seiton (Straighten, or Set in order): neatly arrange what is left, a place for everything and everything in its place.
3. Seiso (Shine): clean and wash; inspect through cleaning so deterioration and leaks are caught early.
4. Seiketsu (Standardize): the cleanliness and order that result from regularly performing the first three Ss, made into a repeatable standard.
5. Shitsuke (Sustain): the discipline to keep performing the first four Ss so gains do not decay.

## The sixth S

Some lean practitioners add a sixth S for Safety: establish and practice safety procedures in the workshop and office.

## Why it matters

5S creates standards that reveal problems, supports the basic stability needed to sustain incremental gains, reduces waste in all forms, and builds a disciplined workplace where teams can focus on value-creating work. The common failure is treating 5S as a one-time cleanup event rather than a sustained daily discipline. Attribution: Lean Enterprise Institute Lean Lexicon.

title: Lean Enterprise Institute, PDCA / Plan-Do-Check-Act (Lean Lexicon)
text:
## PDCA: the improvement cycle

PDCA is an improvement cycle based on the scientific method of proposing a change in a process, implementing the change, measuring the results, and taking appropriate action. It is also called the Deming Cycle or Deming Wheel, after W. Edwards Deming, who introduced it in Japan in the 1950s. It evolved from Walter Shewhart's earlier improvement cycle. PDCA is the foundation of continuous improvement, or kaizen.

## The four steps

1. Plan: determine goals for a process and the changes needed to achieve them. State a hypothesis and predict what will happen.
2. Do: implement the changes, ideally as a small, controlled experiment.
3. Check: evaluate the results against the prediction and the performance target. (In the PDSA variant, this step is Study, emphasizing that you learn from the gap between prediction and result, not just pass or fail it.)
4. Act: if the change worked, standardize and stabilize it as the new standard work; if not, begin the cycle again with what you learned.

## Why it matters

PDCA turns improvement into disciplined experimentation rather than opinion-driven change. Leaders set targets, teams run improvements, results are measured against objectives, and successful changes become standardized work so the gain holds. The classic anti-pattern is skipping Check and Act: teams launch changes (plenty of Plan-Do) but never verify the effect or lock in the win, so improvements neither prove out nor stick. Attribution: Lean Enterprise Institute Lean Lexicon.

title: Lean Enterprise Institute, 5 Whys Root Cause Analysis (Lean Lexicon)
text:
## 5 Whys: reaching the root cause

5 Whys is the practice of asking why repeatedly whenever a problem is encountered, in order to get beyond the obvious symptoms and discover the root cause. It originates with Taiichi Ohno and the Toyota Production System. The specific number five is not the point: the point is to keep asking why until the root cause is reached and eliminated, so the problem cannot recur.

## Taiichi Ohno's machine example

Ohno illustrated the technique with a machine that stopped:
1. Why did the machine stop? A fuse blew because of an overload.
2. Why was there an overload? The bearing was not sufficiently lubricated.
3. Why was it not lubricated enough? The lubrication pump was not pumping sufficiently.
4. Why was it not pumping sufficiently? The pump shaft was worn and rattling.
5. Why was the shaft worn? There was no strainer attached, so metal scraps got in.

Stopping at why two or three (replace the fuse, replace the bearing) fixes the symptom and the machine breaks again. Only the fifth why, install a strainer, prevents recurrence.

## Practicing it well

To use 5 Whys correctly you must first have a clear mental picture of how the process should work and be able to identify exactly where it is misbehaving. It is logic-based root cause analysis: it requires disciplined critical thinking but no advanced mathematics. The aim is always to prevent the problem from recurring by eliminating its underlying cause, not merely to replace the part that failed. Attribution: Lean Enterprise Institute Lean Lexicon.

title: Lean Enterprise Institute, Theory of Constraints (Lean Lexicon)
text:
## Theory of Constraints (TOC)

The Theory of Constraints is a management philosophy and a set of tools for organizational change developed by the Israeli physicist Dr. Eliyahu Goldratt and popularized in his 1984 business novel The Goal. TOC concentrates on improving profit by managing constraints, the factors that prevent a company from achieving its goal.

## Constraint thinking

Every system has at least one constraint, a single bottleneck that limits the throughput of the whole. Improving anywhere other than the constraint does not increase system output; it only creates more inventory or idle capacity. So TOC's primary focus is removing or managing the constraint to improve throughput, whereas lean focuses on identifying and removing waste to improve the flow of value. Both lean and TOC emphasize improving the whole system rather than optimizing individual parts, which is the central discipline that separates real operations leaders from local cost-cutters.

## Relationship to lean

The two philosophies are complementary. Lean makes flow smooth and removes waste everywhere; TOC tells you where in the value stream to concentrate first (the constraint) so that improvement effort converts directly into money. An hour saved at a non-constraint is a mirage; an hour saved at the constraint is an hour of extra throughput for the entire system. Attribution: Lean Enterprise Institute Lean Lexicon.

title: W. Edwards Deming Institute, Deming's 14 Points for Management
text:
## Deming's 14 Points for Management

W. Edwards Deming's 14 Points are the foundation of transforming management for quality. They locate the causes of poor quality in the system, which management owns, not in the individual worker.

1. Create constancy of purpose toward improvement of product and service, with the aim to become competitive, stay in business, and provide jobs.
2. Adopt the new philosophy. Management must awaken to the challenge, learn its responsibilities, and take on leadership for change.
3. Cease dependence on inspection to achieve quality. Eliminate the need for mass inspection by building quality into the product in the first place.
4. End the practice of awarding business on price tag alone. Minimize total cost by moving toward a single supplier for any one item, on a long-term relationship of loyalty and trust.
5. Improve constantly and forever the system of production and service, to improve quality and productivity, and thus constantly decrease costs.
6. Institute training on the job.
7. Institute leadership. The aim of supervision should be to help people and machines do a better job.
8. Drive out fear, so that everyone may work effectively for the company.
9. Break down barriers between departments so research, design, sales, and production work as one team.
10. Eliminate slogans, exhortations, and targets asking the workforce for zero defects and new productivity levels, since the bulk of causes of low quality belong to the system and lie beyond the workforce's power.
11a. Eliminate work standards (quotas) on the factory floor. Substitute leadership.
11b. Eliminate management by objective and management by numbers or numerical goals. Substitute leadership.
12. Remove the barriers that rob workers, and people in management and engineering, of their right to pride of workmanship. This means abolishing the annual merit rating and management by objective.
13. Institute a vigorous program of education and self-improvement.
14. Put everybody in the company to work to accomplish the transformation. The transformation is everybody's job.

## Why an operations leader keeps these close

Points 10, 11, and 12 are the ones most violated in modern operations: numerical quotas, slogans, and merit ratings push people to hit a number by gaming the system rather than improving it. Deming's insight is that exhorting workers to do better cannot fix a system only management can change. Attribution: The W. Edwards Deming Institute.

title: TOC Institute, The Five Focusing Steps (Process of Ongoing Improvement)
text:
## The Five Focusing Steps (POOGI)

Goldratt's Theory of Constraints improves a system through a repeating cycle called the Process of Ongoing Improvement. The guiding image is a chain: the strength of a chain is set by its weakest link, so strengthening any link other than the weakest is a waste of time and energy.

## The five steps

1. Identify the system's constraint. Locate the single limiting factor that currently restricts the whole system's output. Strengthening any link apart from the weakest is wasted effort.
2. Exploit the constraint. Squeeze as much as possible out of it. Maximize the utilization and productivity of the constraint resource before spending any money, for example stop letting the bottleneck sit idle at lunch or process defects, and make sure it only ever works on good, needed parts.
3. Subordinate everything else to the constraint. Align all other processes and policies to support the constraint. Non-constraints must not produce more than the constraint can handle, and must guarantee the constraint never starves for material or attention. This is the step managers hate, because it means deliberately running non-bottlenecks below their full capacity.
4. Elevate the constraint. Only once exploitation and subordination are exhausted do you expand capacity by investing: buy equipment, add a shift, hire people, offload work.
5. Prevent inertia from becoming the constraint. Once elevated, the old weak link may no longer be weakest; a new constraint appears elsewhere. Return to Step 1 and begin the cycle again, and never let policy or habit (inertia) silently become the new constraint.

## Why it matters

The five steps encode the anti-local-optimization discipline: you do not improve everywhere at once, you concentrate on the one place that governs system output, then move to the next. Attribution: TOC Institute.
